title: Indian Heliotrope: How to Spot and Control Buntot Leon in Rice
metaTitle: Indian Heliotrope in Rice: Spot and Control Buntot Leon
metaDescription: Indian heliotrope, or buntot leon, is a hairy broadleaf weed of rainfed rice. Learn to spot its curled flower spike and pull it before it seeds.
excerpt: Indian heliotrope is a hairy broadleaf weed that farmers call buntot leon or elepante. Its small lavender to white flowers grow on a long spike that curls at the tip. You will find it in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it and how it competes with your palay. It also shows how to control it before it drops seed.

blocks.text:
Indian heliotrope is an upright annual herb from the heliotrope family, Heliotropiaceae, once grouped under Boraginaceae. It has many local names. Depending on the area, you may hear ar aritos, bahu baho, buntot leon, elepante, kambra kambra or higad higaran. Several of these names fit its long, curled flower spike, which can look like a tail, a trunk or a caterpillar.

This damo shows up in rainfed lowland rice fields. Being an annual, it lives for only one season. Within a single crop it sprouts, grows, flowers, sets seed and dies. Seed is its only way to spread. The seeds form along the curled spike, then drop to the soil and wait for the next planting. So each plant left standing can seed a whole new patch.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Indian heliotrope
rows: Ar aritos, bahu baho, buntot leon, elepante, kambra kambra, higad higaran

blocks.text: Look for an upright, branching plant with a hairy stem. The leaves are oval to long oval and feel rough when you rub them. Like other broadleaf weeds, the leaves are wide with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. Still, the flowers give it away. Small lavender to white flowers line up on one side of a long spike, and the tip of the spike curls over like a tail.

items: An upright, branched plant with a stem covered in hairs.
Oval leaves with a rough surface that feels like fine sandpaper.
Small lavender to white flowers lined up on only one side of the spike.
A long flower spike that curls at the tip like a tail or a trunk.

blocks.text:
This weed competes with your palay for sunlight, water and fertilizer. It stands upright and branches out, so its rough leaves can shade the young rice near it. In rainfed fields, where water can run short, it takes moisture the crop badly needs. Young rice feels this most, before it can close its canopy.

Because it is an annual that spreads by seed, each plant that flowers adds seed to your soil. That is how one season's weeds become next season's problem. Seeds can also get mixed with the harvested palay. A weedy patch can give insects a place to hide near your rice as well.

items: Pull plants by hand while they are young, before the curled flower spikes appear. Upright plants are easy to grip and pull out.
Once a spike has formed, cut it off first and bag it, then pull the plant. This keeps ripe seeds from dropping in the paddy.
Keep rainwater in the paddy with well kept bunds when you can. Many annual weeds sprout more easily on exposed soil than under water.
Clean the bunds and dry edges of the field. Plants left there can drop seed back into your bukid every season.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Indian heliotrope down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Indian Heliotrope Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Indian Heliotrope?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Indian Heliotrope

items.q: What is Indian heliotrope called in Tagalog and other local names?
items.a: It has many local names. Farmers call it ar aritos, bahu baho, buntot leon, elepante, kambra kambra or higad higaran, depending on the place. Buntot leon means lion's tail, and higad means caterpillar, and both fit its curled flower spike. In English it is Indian heliotrope, and its scientific name is Heliotropium indicum.

items.q: How do I control buntot leon in my rice field?
items.a: Start with prevention. Prepare the land well, use clean binhi, and keep water in the paddy when rain allows. Pull young plants by hand before the flower spikes form. If many plants come up, choose a herbicide for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why do farmers call it elepante or buntot leon?
items.a: The names fit its flower spike. The spike grows long and curls at the tip, much like an elephant trunk or a lion's tail. Small lavender to white flowers line one side of it. This shape is also the easiest way to spot the weed, so use it as your signal to pull the plant before the seeds ripen.
